blocks.body:
## Executive Summary

The completed validation does **not** demonstrate an order-of-magnitude wall-clock speedup for the VUMPS kernel. At the only matched point available—chi=512 and theta/pi=0—the Project B iteration took **381.7 s**, versus a **409.0 s** legacy mean, a modest **1.07x** difference. Against the legacy last-ten-iteration mean of **388.8 s**, the difference is only **1.02x**.

The large gain is instead **about 12x lower node-hour cost**. The legacy allocation was charged as 35 physical cores per wall hour; the recommended 4-logical-CPU, 8-GiB request is charged as 3. That **11.67x lower charge rate** supplies almost all of the savings, while kernel wall time remains broadly similar.

The validation itself finished in 8m24s because it intentionally performed **exactly one** chi=512 iteration after bond-dimension growth. Its ending residual, **6.97e-3**, is far above a production convergence target, so the elapsed job time must not be interpreted as time to obtain a converged chi=512 ground state.

## Matched timing: similar wall time, dramatically lower charge

Using the legacy theta/pi=0 mean gives a projected **0.03106 node-h/iteration** for the old request and **0.002485 node-h/iteration** for Project B, a **12.50x** ratio. This is a resource-efficiency result, not evidence that the numerical kernel became 12.5x faster.

## Why two threads beat a much larger allocation

The controlled chi=256 sweep shows negative scaling beyond two block-sparse threads. **blocksparse-t2** reached **27.77 s/iteration**, versus **36.85 s** for serial-t1 and **57.20 s** for blocksparse-t32. The 32-thread candidate was therefore **2.06x slower in wall time** and **21.97x more expensive per projected iteration** than the winner.

This is consistent with a symmetry-blocked tensor workload: many contractions consist of relatively small independent blocks, so scheduling, synchronization, cache traffic, and NUMA effects can exceed the useful parallel work. More requested cores do not imply more throughput for this kernel.

## Why Project B uses fewer resources

Three implementation choices reduce wasted work: the YC6-1 state now uses the symmetry-compatible **period-2** MPS cell instead of the legacy period-6 supercell; threaded block-sparse contractions are enabled at their measured two-thread sweet spot; and transfer-spectrum eigensolves are separated from optimization so rejected or unconverged states do not automatically pay for 16 eigenvalues at every flux point.

These choices are well motivated, but their individual wall-time contributions are not isolated by the present data. The right-sized Shared-QOS request is the only driver that can be assigned most of the observed node-hour gain quantitatively.

## Why the old campaign felt much slower

The old run's completed finite-flux points averaged roughly **980–1162 s per chi=512 iteration**, versus **409 s** at theta/pi=0. First iterations after flux changes sometimes exceeded **2200–2700 s**, and the workflow also requested 16 transfer eigenvalues at every flux. Those facts explain the 48-hour campaign experience, but they cannot yet be counted as a Project B speedup because no matched finite-flux Project B production run or spectrum benchmark exists.

## Scope and Metric Definitions

- **Matched kernel comparison:** chi=512, theta/pi=0 VUMPS iteration time only. Bond-dimension growth, Julia startup, I/O, and transfer-spectrum postprocessing are excluded.
- **Validation elapsed time:** 503.73 s for the full process, including 57.91 s of growth, 381.74 s of kernel work, and startup/I/O overhead.
- **Projected production cost:** applies the recommended 8-GiB request to measured kernel time. The validation job itself deliberately requested 64 GiB for safety and was charged an estimated 0.019727 node-hours for the whole job.
- **Combined Phase 0 spend:** 0.661567 node-hours for the failed first seed plus 0.432866 for the successful retry, benchmark matrix, and validation, totaling 1.094433 node-hours.

## Methodology

Legacy timing statistics were extracted from all 40 chi=512 VUMPS iteration records at theta/pi=0 in Slurm job 54370665. The Project B validation timing and residual came from `validation.result`; process CPU and memory came from `validation.time`.

Shared-QOS projection follows the Phase 0 script: `charged physical cores = ceil(max(requested logical CPUs, ceil(memory MiB / 1952)) / 2)`, and `node-hours = wall hours x charged physical cores / 128`. Thus the legacy 69-logical-CPU, 128-GiB request maps to 35 charged physical cores, while the recommended 4-logical-CPU, 8-GiB request maps to 3.

At theta/pi=0 this gives 408.951/3600 x 35/128 = **0.0310618 node-hours** for the legacy mean and 381.741/3600 x 3/128 = **0.00248529 node-hours** for Project B.

## Limitations and Robustness

- The new chi=512 kernel estimate has **n=1**; the legacy reference has n=40. No confidence interval is defensible for the new value.
- The new validation residual was 6.97e-3, while the final legacy theta/pi=0 residual was 1.50e-5. Solver state and convergence regime differ.
- The controlled backend sweep was performed at chi=256, not chi=512.
- Unit-cell period, threading backend, thread count, and orchestration all changed together between legacy and Project B, so their individual causal effects cannot be separated from this comparison.
- Legacy MaxRSS and average CPU utilization were not captured locally. The old resource request is known; its actual consumption is not.
- No Project B finite-flux or transfer-spectrum timing is available yet. Those phases may have different scaling and memory requirements.

## Recommendations

1. Use the measured optimization setting for the next pilot: **2 Julia threads, threaded block-sparse enabled, BLAS=1, Strided=1, 4 Slurm logical CPUs, and 8 GiB**. The 1.414-GiB validation MaxRSS leaves 5.66x request headroom.
2. Before a broad flux scan, time **3–5 chi=512 iterations at one nonzero flux** from a checkpoint. Record kernel time, residual movement, MaxRSS, elapsed time, and `sacct` charge. This is the smallest useful test of whether the 2–3x legacy finite-flux slowdown persists.
3. Benchmark transfer-spectrum postprocessing as a separate job. Do not assume the optimization job's 8-GiB memory result automatically covers 16-eigenvalue Krylov solves in multiple spin sectors.
4. Budget production from finite-flux measurements, not from the 8m24s validation elapsed time. Until that measurement exists, keep a **2–3x wall-time contingency** per iteration and checkpoint frequently.
5. Treat the current configuration as selected for efficiency, but retain one matched higher-thread control only if future chi=512 finite-flux data show a clear saturation bottleneck.

## Further Questions

- Does the two-thread optimum remain stable at chi=512 away from theta=0?
- How many iterations does the corrected period-2 state require to meet the production residual gate at each flux?
- What are the time and MaxRSS costs of neutral and spinful transfer-matrix sectors separately?
- Are timings stable across Perlmutter nodes, or is the single validation unusually favorable?
- Once a full corrected scan exists, how much campaign cost is saved by adaptive flux refinement and by postprocessing only accepted states?

query.description: Matched chi=512 theta/pi=0 timing and Perlmutter Shared-QOS charge calculations derived from the Project B validation and legacy Slurm log.
filters: completed legacy flux points for context
metric_definitions: Legacy mean seconds per iteration = arithmetic mean of 40 chi=512 iteration-time records at theta/pi=0.
Charged physical cores = ceil(max(requested logical CPUs, ceil(memory MiB / 1952)) / 2).
Projected node-hours per iteration = seconds per iteration / 3600 x charged physical cores / 128.
Efficiency ratio = legacy projected node-hours per iteration / Project B projected node-hours per iteration.

query.description: Evidence-to-driver assessment separating directly measured effects from implementation changes whose isolated contribution is not identified.
metric_definitions: Causal confidence is qualitative: high only when directly controlled or structurally verified; otherwise the contribution is marked unisolated.

metric_definitions: Budget share percent = combined node-hours / 150 x 100.
Remaining Project B budget = 150 - combined node-hours.
